name: Niche perfume / sample decants

lead: Decants are small portions of a perfume transferred into a vial so you can wear a fragrance for days before paying for a full bottle. Niche perfumery refers to smaller houses whose scents are positioned apart from mass-market designer releases and are often pricier.

By living with a scent on your own skin, you can judge how it smells on you and whether it fits your style before committing. Encyclopedic coverage of the practice is minimal; it is popular in fragrance communities.

paras: People order a few vials of scents they are curious about, wear each across a few days or occasions, and buy a full bottle only for the one they keep reaching for. It is common to rotate several samples before deciding.
As with any fragrance, ingredients can cause skin allergy or breathing irritation in some people. Source and handling of decants vary by seller, so authenticity and storage are the buyer's to judge.

chain: Find a scent that suits you
angle.text: Small vials let you test expensive niche perfumes on your own skin before buying a full bottle, so you settle on a scent that suits you. You then wear a fragrance that fits your style and presentation.

lead: Decants are small portions of a perfume transferred from a full bottle into a small vial, commonly sold so that buyers can test a fragrance before purchasing a full bottle. "Niche" perfumery refers to smaller houses whose products are positioned apart from mass-market designer releases and are often more expensive.

Encyclopedic sources reviewed for this article do not cover decants or niche perfumery directly. Background on perfume composition and concentrations is available: parfum or extrait contains roughly 15 to 30 percent aromatic compounds, eau de parfum about 15 percent and eau de toilette 5 to 15 percent, though houses set their own concentrations.[1]

paras: Natural perfume materials come from plants, animals, lichens and seaweed, while synthetics are produced by a small number of large companies.[1] Because scent labels such as eau de parfum are imprecise and can vary between houses, the same name can denote different strengths.[1]

The Wikipedia perfume article notes an example of a natural-perfumery archive, the Aftel Archive of Curious Scents, focusing on botanical materials.[1] Decant services themselves are not covered by it.

Fragrance communities discuss decants as a way to try expensive scents without full-bottle purchases. Specific community sources were not available for citation, and no information about pricing, authenticity or storage practices is given here.
Fragrance ingredients can trigger skin allergies, headaches and asthma reactions in some people.[1] Perfume contents are rarely disclosed in full, as companies cite trade secrets.[1]
